newsitem.title: UK: EMU jitters keep dollar in demand in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: EMU jitters keep dollar in demand in late Europe.

text.p: The dollar was glowing from its trip to four-week highs in late Europe, reaping dividends from market confusion over France's political swing to the left.
As Socialist Lionel Jospin became France's new prime minister, the market was beset by fears the left's election victory would mean a broad, weak euro or a delay to EMU.
Though EMU delay is usually seen as mark-positive, analysts said the generally uncertain climate would benefit the dollar.
"The bottom line is that whatever the scenarios are in Europe, there is a much greater degree of uncertainty premium to be placed on European assets," said Stephen Hannah at IBJ here.

Though market concerns were concentrated on the prospect of a soft euro on Monday, analysts said the mark should begin to reassert itself if market expectations grow to favour delay. That prospect was keeping the dollar from topping its 1997 high of 1.7389 marks, said Hannah, director of research at IBJ.
The dollar was trading at 1.7280/90 marks at 1542 GMT, two pfennigs up from late Friday's European level of 1.7082/92. It earlier glanced 1.7310 marks, its strongest rate since May 6.
Expectations France will push for a broader euro were fueled by French Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande, who called for Italy and Spain to be included in EMU.
Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet insisted that the euro would bear the legacy of the most solid ERM currencies, and said EMU would foster structural reform and growth in Europe.
But the market was more inclined to listen to officials like Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister, who said the EMU project may enter "rougher waters" in the weeks and months ahead.

"Europe as a collective against the rest of the world is sending out the message it's going to devalue itself relative to the dollar and the yen and sterling to get itself out of trouble and reflate itself," said Chris Tinker, chief treasury economist at Standard Chartered here.
The ongoing dispute between Germany's government and central bank over Bonn's plans to revalue its assets to help qualify for EMU will also underpin the dollar, analysts said.

Three Bundesbank members stepped up their criticism of the plan on Monday. Meantime, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he hoped to reach agreement with the bank but vowed the government would not retreat from its plan.

An added bonus for the dollar was a data release showing the U.S. National Association of Purchasing Managers index jumped to 57.1 in May, well up from April's reading of 54.2 and average market expectations of 53.9.
Analysts noted hefty increases in the NAPM new orders and supplier deliveries indices, and said that suggested a strong underlying pace of economic activity in the United States.
And they were further cheered by a fall in the NAPM inflation index to 48.4 from April's 49.6.

Other U.S. data showed a meagre 0.1 percent rise in April personal income and spending and a 1.0 percent fall in April construction spending where the market had been predicting a 0.3 percent increase.
This week's major U.S. data focus, however, is firmly on the non-farm payrolls figure for May, which will appear on Friday.
Strong economic data are seen boosting the dollar as they fuel talk of higher U.S. interest rates, especially as recent Japanese rate-rise speculation simmers down.
For now, though, dollar/yen is clearly sidelined. It stood at 116.55/65 at 1612 GMT compared to late Friday's 116.37/47.
Sterling/mark stormed ahead, matching dollar/mark's four-week highs, to trade at 2.8225/35 versus 2.7960/75 on Friday.
The Swiss franc, though also viewed as a safe haven from EMU turmoil, struggled to make headway against the mark as dollar/Swiss jumped to around 1.43 from Friday's 1.4145/55.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
